title: EdgeFleet - p95 / Concurrency / Token Benchmark Discovery
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment
next_steps: Redwood to share initial token/sec benchmark plan and test harness
EdgeFleet to provide representative prompt corpus and peak qps windows
Schedule dedicated performance run next week (2 hour slot)
action_items: Maya: send benchmark spreadsheet + runner details by 2026-04-08
Liam: upload 2k sample prompts and 5 head-of-day peak traces by 2026-04-09
Daniel: propose dedicated cluster sizing options by 2026-04-10
summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency goals (50-120ms for short completion), concurrency patterns, streaming token rates, and tradeoffs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. Customer is evaluating for a customer-facing assistant with bursty traffic and strict data residency requirements.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're on the record. Quick intro — I'm Maya, AE on the account. With me is Daniel, our SE, and Jordan from solutions.
[00:12] Aria Gomez: Hi, Aria here — CTO at EdgeFleet. We have Liam, Sofia, and Ben on the call. Thanks for fitting us in.
[00:20] Maya: Great. High level, we want to understand your latency SLOs, throughput patterns, and where Redwood fits (hosted/dedicated/private). Could you start with the product context?
[00:33] Aria: Sure. We're building an operator assistant embedded in our telematics dashboard — real time-ish suggestions, mostly short completions 30-80 tokens, sometimes longer when summarizing trips. Target p95 is, ideally, sub-100ms for the short flows, but we can tolerate up to 200-300ms for heavier summaries.
[00:52] Liam O'Connor: To add, peak concurrent users during fleet check-ins can be around 1.2k simultaneous sessions, but that's spread across regions. Burstiness is the issue: during morning rollcall we see 4-5x baseline for ~7 minutes. So tokens/sec spikes matter.
[01:08] Daniel Kim: Thanks. When you say 'sub-100ms p95' for short flows, is that end-to-end from client to response? Any pre/post-processing budget?
[01:18] Sofia Ruiz: Yes end-to-end. We have about 15ms on client side, and 10-20ms for light enrichment. So we need service <80ms ideally.
[01:27] Maya: Understood. Quick clarifying question: are you more interested in streaming token-by-token to the client, or do you serve the full completion in one go?
[01:35] Ben Tran: We currently stream for long summaries, but for the short suggestions we prefer single-shot — lower overhead. However, streaming could help perceived latency.
[01:45] Daniel: Right, streaming reduces time-to-first-token but can add complexity to SLOs. Also affects batching and throughput. For benchmarking we should separate: TTF (time to first token), and time to final token and p95 both for TTF and final.
[02:00] Aria: That sounds reasonable. We want both metrics.
[02:05] Maya: Cool. Can you describe your current stack? Model sizes, on-prem dependencies, and data residency constraints?
[02:13] Liam: We're using a mix of open models — mid-size, mostly 7B-ish for suggestion path, 13B for summaries. Currently hosted on our cloud but behind strict VPC peering and we have encryption keys in our KMS. We need SOC2 and ISO27001 assurance; some customers ask for on-prem options.
[02:32] Daniel: Got it — thanks. A few notes up front: Hosted Redwood can hit low-latency tails for small models with efficient kernels; Dedicated gives you predictable capacity and isolated GPU pools; Private (VPC or on-prem) gives you the residency and KMS control but requires onboarding & sizing.
[02:50] Maya: For the p95 numbers you mentioned (50-100ms), that's aggressive but not impossible for 7B in hosted if you want single-token responses. Sequence length, batching, KV cache hits matter a lot.
[03:03] Liam: Could you expand on KV cache and prefix caching? We have a lot of repeated prompts (templates), curious how much caching helps.
[03:11] Daniel: Sure. If you have repeated prefixes or shared context — say system prompt + few-shot examples — Redwood can cache KV states to avoid recomputing early layers. We call it KV cache and prefix caching. In practice, for repeated templates you can get 20-60% lower token compute in the steady state; numbers vary.
[03:29] Sofia: But how does that interact with streaming? If you start streaming, do you still get the same savings?
[03:34] Daniel: Generally yes — cache reduces per-token compute even with streaming. But streaming may reduce our ability to batch across requests because we often flush earlier to emit tokens. So there's a tradeoff: streaming improves perceived latency (TTF) but can hurt throughput at high concurrency.
[03:49] Aria: For our workload, morning burst with 5x concurrent short calls — what's a realistic approach? Dedicated? Hosted with autoscaling? Private?
[03:58] Maya: For predictable burst patterns, Dedicated often fits: you reserve baseline capacity and we can allow short burst capacity. Hosted can handle it too but might have variable p95 during the exact burst window unless we pin to dedicated instances or use auto-burst provisions. Private requires capacity planning on your side.
[04:16] Liam: We're leaning to Dedicated because of the SLA and data assurances. Can you outline sizing? For 1.2k concurrent sessions, most short completions ~40 tokens, what's the tokens/sec we'd expect?
[04:27] Daniel: Rough calc: 1.2k concurrent * 40 tokens = 48k in-flight tokens if all generating simultaneously. But in practice concurrency isn't all generating at same time due to think time. For steady-state throughput we look at tokens/sec peak. If you see bursts of, say, 500 qps with 40 tokens => 20k tokens/sec.
[04:45] Jordan Lee: Right. Our benchmarks use tokens/sec per GPU metric. For 7B quantized on A100-ish class, you might see anywhere from 8k-18k tokens/sec depending on sequence lengths, batching, and beam/temperature settings.
[04:59] Maya: We'll propose a benchmark run that simulates your morning rollcall pattern: 7 minute window with 4-5x baseline, mix of 70% short suggestions (30-50 tokens) and 30% longer summaries (200-400 tokens) and both streaming and non-streaming paths.
[05:15] Aria: That would be perfect. Also include TTF p50/p95 and final token p95.
[05:22] Daniel: We'll also measure tail on a per-route basis, and instrument prefix cache hit rates.
[05:27] Ben: On security — can you explain how KMS and key management works in Dedicated vs Hosted? Are the keys in Redwood KMS or can we keep keys in our cloud KMS?
[05:38] Maya: Good question. Hosted uses our key management; for Dedicated we support customer-managed keys via KMS integrations (bring your own key). Private obviously allows keys fully in-customer control — we integrate with your HSM/KMS over VPC. We'll share our security pack.
[05:53] Sofia: Compliance-wise, do you provide audit logs for every token/request? We need traceability for certain customers.
[06:00] Daniel: Yes — request-level audit logs, model version, latency, token counts. Log retention is configurable and we have SOC2 artifacts. For Private deployments we can forward logs to your SIEM.
[06:13] Aria: Cost is also a factor. We want unit economics. How will you report tokens/cost during the benchmark?
[06:20] Jordan: We'll provide token-level cost estimates against hosted pricing and a breakdown for Dedicated (amortized GPU + infra + egress). Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization or batching to improve unit-cost with minimal impact to quality.
[06:33] Liam: For benchmarking, can we run noise tests to see p95 under noisy co-tenancy?
[06:38] Daniel: Yes, we can simulate background load or noisy neighbors. For Dedicated you can get stronger isolation; hosted will have more variability though we do hot-path isolation for premium tiers.
[06:50] Aria: I want to make sure we capture third-party latency — network hops from our VPC peering. Could that add 10-20ms?
[06:58] Sofia: We saw 18ms roundtrip in a naive test.
[07:02] Daniel: Network adds always factor in. In our lab runs we also do an end-to-end test from a customer endpoint to capture that delta.
[07:10] Maya: Ok next, scheduling: we'd like to run a 2-hour dedicated benchmark next Tuesday. What prep do you need from our side?
[07:18] Maya: (cont.) Specifically, can you provide sample prompts, region preference, and expected peak windows?
[07:23] Liam: We'll upload a corpus of 2k prompts (mixed). We'll also provide traces of qps with timestamp buckets and the regions (US-west and EU-west).
[07:33] Maya: Great. We'll also ask you to confirm model variants: 7B for suggestions, 13B for summaries. Any preference on quantization?
[07:42] Liam: We want to start with FP16 if possible, and then test 4-bit quant later to see quality tradeoffs.
[07:49] Daniel: Noted. We'll run FP16 baseline and a 4-bit quantized pass. We'll report perplexity/ROUGE or sample quality delta if you have eval prompts.
[07:59] Ben: One more question — routing/fallbacks. If a Dedicated pool is saturated do you automatically fall back to Hosted? We need predictable behavior.
[08:07] Maya: We support smart routing policies — you can set hard fallbacks to a lower-capacity hosted tier or queue requests. We can also configure rate limiting and graceful degradation strategies.
[08:17] Aria: Sounds good. Let's summarize next steps.
[08:20] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send benchmark plan + runner + cost spreadsheet. EdgeFleet to provide 2k prompt corpus, qps traces, and preferred test windows. We'll schedule the 2-hour run and then review results with a follow-up. Also share security pack.
[08:35] Liam: Timeline looks good. We'll aim to get artifacts to you by end of day tomorrow.
[08:40] Sofia: One last small item — can you include guidance on canary rollouts and model pinning?
[08:45] Daniel: Absolutely. We'll include configuration examples for canary percentages, A/B, and automatic rollback on quality regressions tied to prompt eval sets.
[08:54] Maya: Perfect. Any final questions?
[08:57] Aria: No, that's it. Thanks.
[09:00] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the deck and benchmark steps.
[09:05] [call ends — 52:01 total]
